newsitem.title: INDIA: India's image problems deter foreign investors.
newsitem.headline: India's image problems deter foreign investors.

text.p: Poor infrastructure, rampant red-tape and mismatched corporate expectations deter many foreign investors from putting their money in India, speakers at a conference on foreign direct investment said on Thursday.
"The Indian government's red-tape is cumbersome, time-consuming and complicated," said Sakutaro Tanino, the Japanese ambassador to New Delhi.
Foreign direct investment (FDI) inflow to India was around $2 billion in 1995/96, according to official figures.
India wants to boost FDI to at least $10 billion annually.
"This amount of FDI inflow may look ambitious against the inflow of $2 billion achieved last year," said Industries Minister Murasoli Muran.
"However, the experience of China and other East Asian countries proves the target of $10 billion is achievable keeping in mind the fundamental strengths of our economy."
Other speakers felt this might be difficult.
"$10 billion is a tough target," said Jonathan Bensky, commercial counsellor at the U.S. embassy in New Delhi. "But it's good for the reach to exceed the grasp."
Government delays in approving projects sometimes forced American firms to drop them, Bensky said.

Protests in India that blocked work on a 2,450 MW plant by U.S. energy giant Enron for almost a year and forced Kentucky Fried Chicken to suspend operations could discourage many potential U.S. investors, Bensky said.
"You may not appreciate how widely news of Enron and Kentucky Fried Chicken has spread in the U.S.," he said.
"Many companies will look at that and take it as symbolic of India's attitude to foreign investment. Whether it is true or not, reality is in the eye of the beholder."
India's infrastructure deficiencies also discouraged investors, Japanese ambassador Tanino said.
"There is a serious need to take immediate steps to expand and upgrade infrastructure facilities like power generation and distribution, telecommunications, roads and ports," he said.
Bensky said some American firms had entered into joint ventures with Indian companies only to find they had serious differences in outlook.

Indian firms tended to have shorter profit horizons, perhaps 14 to 18 months, as compared to American firms, which did not expect profits for four or five years until they had established themselves, Bensky said.
But Indian FDI levels exceeded Chinese FDI levels at roughly the same stage in the reforms process, said Anthony Smith, charge d'affaires at the European Commission delegation in India.

"Actual FDI in India in the first five years of reforms exceeds the level of FDI in China in the corresponding period, a fact usually overlooked when comparing the performance of the two Asian giants in this field," Smith said.
The European Union's share of FDI inflows to India was 16.85 percent in 1994-95 (April-March), Smith said, as compared to 14.85 percent for the U.S., and 4.95 percent for Japan.
